### Step 1: Understand the problem and key idea

- We seek the maximum possible order of an element of $S_{10}$.
- The order of a permutation equals the least common multiple (lcm) of the lengths of its disjoint cycles.
- The cycle lengths must be positive integers summing to $10$.
- So we must choose a partition of $10$ whose parts' lcm is as large as possible.

  

### Step 2: Consider plausible partitions and their lcms

- Single cycle: $10$ gives order $10$.
- Two cycles:
  - $7 + 3$: $$\text{lcm}(7,3)=21$$
  - $6 + 4$: $$\text{lcm}(6,4)=12$$
  - $8 + 2$: $$\text{lcm}(8,2)=8$$
  - $5 + 5$: $$\text{lcm}(5,5)=5$$
- Three cycles:
  - $5 + 3 + 2$: $$\text{lcm}(5,3,2)=\text{lcm}(5,3)=15\times2/\gcd(15,2)=30\quad\Rightarrow\quad30$$
  - $4 + 3 + 3$: $$\text{lcm}(4,3,3)=\text{lcm}(4,3)=12$$
  - $6 + 3 + 1$: $$\text{lcm}(6,3,1)=6$$

  $$\operatorname{lcm}(9,1)=9$$

  $$\operatorname{lcm}(6,4)=12$$

- Partition $10 = 6 + 3 + 1$  

  $$\operatorname{lcm}(6,3,1)=\operatorname{lcm}(6,3)=6$$

- Partition $10 = 4 + 3 + 3$  

  $$\operatorname{lcm}(4,3,3)=\operatorname{lcm}(4,3)=12$$

- Partition $10 = 5 + 5$  

  $$\operatorname{lcm}(5,5)=5$$

- (Other partitions with more 1's only reduce the lcm or match one of the above cases.)
